items.stem: Read a memoir extract, ‘The River’. ‘I learned to swim in the brown river behind my uncle’s house the summer I was nine. There was no teacher, no float, no shallow end; there was only my cousin Bilal, who was eleven and therefore an expert. “Just kick,” he said, and let go of my hands. I sank like a stone. Under the water everything turned green and silent, and I remember thinking, quite calmly, that this was a strange place to end up. Then Bilal’s hand closed around my collar and hauled me into the air. I coughed half the river onto the bank. “Again,” he said. Looking back now, I am amazed that either of us was allowed near that water. But by the end of August I could swim to the far bank and back, and I have never since felt quite so proud.’ How does the writer present the experience of learning to swim?
items.answer: Humorous, affectionate tone; Bilal as a comic, determined teacher; vivid sensory moment underwater; hyperbole; adult reflection (Looking back now); pride at the end.
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (3–4) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [4]

items.stem: Read an extract from a biography of the (fictional) engineer Hana Sato. ‘Hana Sato was born in 1961 in a fishing village on the coast of Japan, the youngest of five children. Her father repaired boat engines, and by the age of eight Hana could strip down an outboard motor faster than most of his customers. At school she was quiet, often in trouble for taking apart the classroom clock. In 1983 she became one of only two women to graduate in mechanical engineering from her university that year. Her breakthrough came in 1998, when she designed a low-cost water pump that could be repaired with a bicycle spanner. Instead of selling it to large companies, she published the design for free. Today the pump is used in more than forty countries. “An invention nobody can fix,” she once said, “is only half an invention.”’ (a) When did Hana Sato have her breakthrough? (b) How does the biographer present Hana Sato as an admirable person?
items.answer: (a) 1998 (b) Chronological structure; early anecdotes of talent; achievement against the odds (one of two women); practical genius (bicycle spanner); generosity (free design); impact (forty countries); her own words.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: 1998 [1] (b) Level-marked: top band (3–4) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [4]

items.stem: Text A is an extract from a biography of the (fictional) engineer Hana Sato: ‘Hana Sato was born in 1961 in a fishing village on the coast of Japan, the youngest of five children. Her father repaired boat engines, and by the age of eight Hana could strip down an outboard motor faster than most of his customers. At school she was quiet, often in trouble for taking apart the classroom clock. In 1983 she became one of only two women to graduate in mechanical engineering from her university that year. Her breakthrough came in 1998, when she designed a low-cost water pump that could be repaired with a bicycle spanner. Instead of selling it to large companies, she published the design for free. Today the pump is used in more than forty countries. “An invention nobody can fix,” she once said, “is only half an invention.”’ Text B is an autobiography extract, ‘Arrival’: ‘The first thing I noticed about Toronto was the cold. It was not the friendly cold of a fridge door opened on a hot day in Lahore; it was a cold with teeth. My father had bought us coats from a market before we left, thin padded things that the wind went straight through. At my new school, the teacher said my name wrongly, and I was too shy to correct her, so for two whole years I answered to a name that was not quite mine. I did not speak in class for a month. Then one afternoon a girl called Grace asked if she could borrow my eraser, and when I answered, she said, “Oh! You talk!” and laughed, and suddenly so did I. We are still friends. She still has my eraser.’ Explain two differences between the ways the two texts are written, linked to their type of life writing.
items.answer: Text A is a biography (third person, researched facts, chronological, quotation from the subject); Text B is a autobiography (first person, the writer’s own experiences, reflection). Differences may include person (first/third), use of reflection versus facts and dates, tone and use of quotation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 per valid difference with evidence from both texts; further marks for linking features to the purpose of each type.

items.stem: This extract is from a diary: ‘Monday 3 March. Rained again. Mum says we might move house.’ Explain two features that show this.
items.answer: Diary: date heading, note-like, immediate.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying diary; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: date heading, note-like, immediate.

items.stem: Identify the type of life writing in this extract, explain the features that show it, and rewrite the sentence as a different type (e.g. biography into autobiography): ‘Dear Diary, Today was the worst day of term. Tomorrow will be better, I hope.’
items.answer: Diary: dated, private, informal entry written as things happen. The rewrite should change person and/or tense and tone appropriately.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for the type (diary); 1 for supporting features; remaining mark(s) for an accurate rewrite in a different form.

items.stem: Write a memoir about a place you have left behind. Include vivid detail of the experience and reflection on what it meant to you. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: opening at a vivid moment; context; the key incident with sensory detail and dialogue; turning point; reflection (‘Looking back…’) on what a place you have left behind taught you.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): a vivid, selective account with a clear chronology; reflection on the significance of the experience woven in; a distinctive personal voice; middle band (3–4): a clear account with some detail and some reflection; personal voice present; lower band (1–2): a list of events with little detail or reflection. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: focused, selected moments; sensory detail; remembered dialogue; reflective comments showing hindsight; ending that links past to present.

items.stem: Which technique is used in this line from an autobiography extract, ‘Arrival’? ‘I did not speak in class for a month.’
items.answer: Short sentence
items.markingKey: Short sentence: a deliberately brief sentence that stands out. Here ‘I did not speak in class for a month.’ – the plain sentence emphasises the writer’s isolation and silence.

items.stem: In an extract from a biography of the (fictional) engineer Hana Sato the writer writes: ‘Instead of selling it to large companies, she published the design for free.’ What does this suggest about Hana Sato’s values?
items.answer: She cared more about helping people than about money; she wanted the pump to be available to everyone.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: generous/idealistic; reference to choosing free publication over profit

items.stem: Read ‘I sank like a stone.’ from a memoir extract, ‘The River’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Simile (‘like a stone’): the short, blunt comparison captures how suddenly and helplessly the child went under, with some humour.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (simile); 1 for selecting the key words ‘like a stone’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the short, blunt comparison captures how suddenly and helplessly the child went under, with some humour.

items.stem: Read ‘It was not the friendly cold of a fridge door opened on a hot day in Lahore’ from an autobiography extract, ‘Arrival’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Contrast (‘the friendly cold of a fridge door’): comparing the pleasant cold of home with the harsh new cold shows the writer’s homesickness.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (contrast); 1 for selecting the key words ‘the friendly cold of a fridge door’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. comparing the pleasant cold of home with the harsh new cold shows the writer’s homesickness.

items.stem: Here are extracts from two pieces of life writing. Text A (a memoir extract, ‘The River’): ‘Looking back now, I am amazed that either of us was allowed near that water.’ … ‘who was eleven and therefore an expert’ Text B (an autobiography extract, ‘Arrival’): ‘I was too shy to correct her, so for two whole years I answered to a name that was not quite mine’ … ‘We are still friends. She still has my eraser.’ Compare how the two writers present the way the writers make people and events vivid for the reader. Refer closely to language and structure in both texts.
items.answer: Text A: Humorous, affectionate tone; Bilal as a comic, determined teacher; vivid sensory moment underwater; hyperbole; adult reflection (Looking back now); pride at the end. Text B: Metaphor of cold with teeth; contrast with home; detail of thin coats; lost name; silence; turning point with Grace; humour and warmth in the ending. Comparison of how each presents the way the writers make people and events vivid for the reader, with reference to person, tone, structure and language.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Text A: Humorous, affectionate tone; Bilal as a comic, determined teacher; vivid sensory moment underwater; hyperbole; adult reflection (Looking back now); pride at the end. Text B: Metaphor of cold with teeth; contrast with home; detail of thin coats; lost name; silence; turning point with Grace; humour and warmth in the ending. Comparison of how each presents the way the writers make people and events vivid for the reader, with reference to person, tone, structure and language.

items.stem: In a recount, the writer revises ‘We got lost on the mountain and found the path at sunset.’ into ‘We got lost on the mountain and found the path at sunset, and I think that was when I first realised my father did not know everything – and that this was all right.’ How does this change help the reader understand the experience?
items.answer: It turns a bare event into a meaningful memory: the older writer looks back and explains what the experience taught them, so the reader understands its significance.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: shows hindsight or a change in understanding; explains the significance or lesson of the event; links past and present self.

items.stem: A memoir writer changes ‘I forgot my lines in the school play.’ to ‘I forgot my lines in the school play; at the time it felt like the end of the world, but it was the first time I learned that people forgive mistakes faster than we do.’ Explain what the added reflection does for the reader.
items.answer: It turns a bare event into a meaningful memory: the older writer looks back and explains what the experience taught them, so the reader understands its significance.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: shows hindsight or a change in understanding; explains the significance or lesson of the event; links past and present self.

items.stem: Add reflection to this sentence from a recount so that it shows what the experience meant to the writer. ‘I broke my arm falling off my bike.’
items.answer: Model: ‘I broke my arm falling off my bike, and those six weeks of one-handed life taught me more about patience than any lesson ever had.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: reflective phrase (looking back, I realise, only later); a clear insight; accurate expression. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Write the opening paragraph of a memoir about a time you were afraid but did something anyway. Include at least two sensory details and end with one sentence of reflection that looks back from the present.
items.answer: Model: begins at a vivid moment in the past tense, with sight/sound/smell details, and ends with a reflective present-tense sentence (e.g. ‘Even now, I can see…’ or ‘I did not know then that…’).
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: vivid opening moment; two or more sensory details; reflective final sentence showing hindsight; accurate tense control.

items.stem: Write a memoir about the first time you were trusted with responsibility. Include vivid detail of the experience and reflection on what it meant to you. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model structure: opening at a vivid moment; context; the key incident with sensory detail and dialogue; turning point; reflection (‘Looking back…’) on what the first time you were trusted with responsibility taught you.
